images.title: A strip of factors becomes a power
images.purpose: Shows the core move of the practice tool: a strip of four 6s is written as 6⁴ and multiplied out to 1296.
images.composition: Plain white background, lots of empty space around the main object, no scenery, no people, no extra text. One row of factor blocks across the centre with a brace below, and an arrow to the power form and its value on the right.
images.exact_structure: Exactly 4 equal square teal (#0072B2) blocks in a row, each showing '6', with a '×' sign in each of the 3 gaps between them. A thin amber (#E69F00) brace under all four blocks with the label '4 factors' under it. To the right, a thick amber (#E69F00) arrow pointing right to the power '6⁴' in large type, then a thin arrow to the value '1296' inside a reddish purple (#CC79A7) rounded box. Exactly 4 blocks, 3 times signs, 1 brace, 2 arrows, 1 box.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec

images.takeaway: Count the equal factors to get the exponent, then multiply to get the value.
images.description: Shows the core move of the practice tool: a strip of four 6s is written as 6⁴ and multiplied out to 1296.
images.context: 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 = 1296 = 6⁴. The practice also covers prime factor forms such as 648 = 2³ × 3⁴.
images.teaching_notes: Label '6' appears on 4 blocks and '×' in 3 gaps.

image_decisions.why: The practice tool turns a strip of factors into a power and a value; this picture shows that manipulation in its simplest state.
